extracted.intended_audience: IP law firms, designers, innovators, and businesses seeking international industrial design protection
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for preparing and filing an international design application under the WIPO Hague System, including eligibility, formalities, fees, publication, post-filing steps, and maintenance across multiple jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant eligibility (connection to member country)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be eligible for the Hague System, applicants must have a connection to at least one of the member countries: be a national of a member country, have a domicile or habitual residence there, or maintain a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment within its territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentarea helps assess eligibility and prepare filings based on jurisdiction and business structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: What may be protected (ornamental aspects only)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague System protects the ornamental aspects of industrial products (shapes, lines, textures, colors, surface ornamentation, and combinations of these elements); functional aspects are not protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the subject matter is a visual/design feature rather than a functional invention before using the Hague route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of designs per application and Locarno class requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An international application can include up to 100 different designs provided they fall within the same class of the Locarno Classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group only designs in the same Locarno class in a single filing; otherwise file separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required applicant/contact information and eligibility indication
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must include the name and address of the applicant and a clear indication of the applicant’s eligibility under the Hague Agreement (e.g., nationality, residence, establishment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurately state the basis for eligibility to avoid formal objections or invitations to correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representations (drawings or photographs) and product indication
rubrics_metrics.description: Each design must include a clear representation (drawings or photographs) and a brief product indication describing the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also provide a list of designated countries for protection alongside the representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and format of drawings/photographs
rubrics_metrics.description: Representations must be clear, consistent, and complete, showing the design from all relevant angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poor-quality or inconsistent images risk a WIPO invitation to correct irregularities; follow WIPO drawing formalities (see Design Application Full Guide).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application language and electronic filing
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must be filed in English, French, or Spanish and submitted electronically via WIPO’s eHague system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English is highly recommended. Use eHague to ensure correct submission and faster processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: WIPO formal (administrative) examination scope
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO performs a formal examination only to ensure administrative requirements are met (image quality, completeness, and correct fee payment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If deficiencies are found, WIPO may issue an invitation to correct irregularities within a specified period (typically three months).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction period for formal irregularities
rubrics_metrics.description: If formalities are deficient, applicants typically have a specified period (typically three months) to correct irregularities after WIPO's invitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely correction avoids rejection and allows the application to proceed to registration and publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation of countries and national-phase examinations
rubrics_metrics.description: After international publication, each designated country may conduct its own substantive examination according to national law and may issue a statement of grant or a notification of refusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect different outcomes per country; plan for national responses and possible refusals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timing and options (immediate, standard, deferred)
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered designs are recorded in the International Register and published in the International Designs Bulletin; publication generally takes place six months after registration, but applicants may request early or deferred publication (deferment up to 30 months in some countries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use publication timing strategically to align with market launch or confidentiality strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee structure and cost considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing international design applications involves filing, publication, and designation fees. The filing fee is fixed; publication fees depend on immediate/standard/deferred publication; designation fees vary by country; totals depend on number of designs and designations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate official fees using WIPO’s Fee Calculator and factor in local agent costs for national phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countries covered and limits of the Hague System
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague System covers more than 150 jurisdictions (including US, EU, UK, China, Japan, etc.), but not all countries are members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If target markets are not members, coordinate Patentarea or local agents for direct national filings to ensure full protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to consider international design protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider Hague filing when commercializing a product in multiple countries, when design is critical to brand identity or competitive advantage, when licensing or manufacturing abroad, or when targeting markets with common design infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing through the Hague System allows fast, strategic action across many territories with one application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local representation and coordination for national issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Appoint a local patent attorney in each jurisdiction where protection is sought—particularly in countries that issue refusals or require local representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentarea coordinates with trusted local agents worldwide to respond to objections and comply with formalities; plan for local agent fees and response timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration, renewals, and maximum terms
rubrics_metrics.description: International registrations are valid initially for five years and may be renewed for additional five-year periods up to the maximum term allowed in each designated country (some countries allow protection for up to 15, 20, or 25 years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renewals are handled through WIPO, simplifying maintenance across multiple jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized post-filing management via WIPO
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-filing tasks such as renewals, changes of ownership, and address updates can be managed centrally through WIPO rather than individual national offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralization reduces administrative overhead and streamlines maintenance, but monitor national requirements and deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of direct national filings when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: For countries not covered by the Hague System, direct national filings are required to secure design protection in those jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentarea provides support for direct national filings to ensure complete global protection when the Hague System does not reach target markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic advantages of the Hague System
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague System simplifies registration with a single application and payment in one currency, centralizes post-filing tasks, and allows control over publication timing, making it a cost-effective and time-saving solution for multi-jurisdictional design protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh these advantages against national filing strategies and local enforcement realities when planning global design protection.
